sources.title: Syria declares ceasefire in parts of Aleppo after days of clashes
sources.evidenceText: The Syrian government announced a ceasefire in several neighborhoods of Aleppo early Friday after days of deadly clashes between Syrian forces and Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). In a statement, the Syrian Defense Ministry said the ceasefire was introduced “to prevent any slide towards a new military escalation within residential neighborhoods.” The truce took effect at 3:00 a.m. local time and covers the Sheikh Maqsoud, Ashrafieh, and Bani Zeid districts of northern Aleppo. The ministry emphasized that the decision is part of broader efforts to de-escalate tensions and stabilize the situation in the city. According to the announcement, internal security forces, working alongside the Syrian army, will oversee mechanisms for the withdrawal of armed groups from the affected neighborhoods toward northeastern Syria. Authorities said the move aims to restore calm, reestablish state authority, and prepare conditions for the return of civilian life and rule of law in the impacted areas, following several days of violence that heightened fears of renewed urban conflict in Aleppo. The clashes had raised regional concern due to Aleppo’s history as one of the most contested battlegrounds of Syria’s long-running conflict. Further details on implementation of the ceasefire and the timeline for withdrawals have yet to be released. A fierce exchange of fire extended into the night, with rescue workers scrambling to extinguish fires ignited by shelling, before the Defence Ministry said it would give armed groups a six-hour window on Friday to leave the contested areas. In a statement, the ministry said the ceasefire in the neighbourhoods of Sheikh Maqsoud, Ashrafieh and Bani Zaid from 3am (00:00 GMT) would ”pave the way for the restoration of law and official institutions and to protect civilians”. The window for the SDF to withdraw closes at 9am and departing fighters will be permitted to carry “personal light weapons”, state news agency SANA reported, citing the Defence Ministry. Aleppo’s media directorate said on Friday that SDF fighters encircled by the Syrian army in two districts of the city are to be sent to the Kurdish-majority region of northeastern Syria. “In the coming hours, members of the SDF will be moved with their light weapons to the east of the Euphrates [river],” it said. However, Kurdish councils in Syria’s Aleppo said on Friday they would not ⁠evacuate neighbourhoods under their control. In a statement published by Syrian Kurdish ‌outlets, the local councils of the Ashrafieh and Sheikh Maqsoud ‌districts said calls to ‌leave Aleppo ⁠were “a call to surrender” and that Kurdish-led forces would ‌instead “defend their neighbourhoods”. The United States had earlier welcomed the ceasefire announcement in a post on X by its envoy Tom Barrack. He said Washington hoped for “a more enduring calm and deeper dialogue” and was “working intensively to extend this ceasefire and spirit of understanding”. The Kurdish-led group has denied the allegations, saying this week’s casualties were caused by “indiscriminate” artillery and missile shelling by factions aligned with the government in Damascus. The clashes come as talks on how to implement a March 2025 agreement to integrate the SDF, which has controlled large swaths of territory in Syria’s north and northeast, into the country’s state institutions faltered. sources.imageAlt: Dutch minister of finance Eelco Heinen attends the Eurozone finance ministers meeting in Luxembourg. Photo: Olivier Hoslet/EPA
sources.evidenceText: When the EU’s finance ministers sat down for a working dinner in Luxembourg last Thursday evening, Simon Harris warned his counterparts they could be about to face another day of newspaper headlines bashing Europe for again ducking a big decision. Or, they could strike a deal, even if the compromise on the table wasn’t perfect, the Irish Minister for Finance said. Finance officials had been toiling for months over a contentious package of reforms intended to break a decade long logjam. The proposals would shift more responsibility for regulating the architecture that makes the financial markets tick from national central banks and authorities to a European regulator. Simplifying this layer of oversight would hopefully make it easier for investment cash and funding to flow across national borders, ideally creating a bigger pool of European capital that businesses could tap to raise investment and expand. The Irish Government had set itself a tight deadline when taking over the Council of the EU presidency in July. It wanted to agree a deal on the hugely technical package of financial legislation by the October meeting of EU finance ministers. Harris, who would be chairing discussions during the EU presidency, had gone back and forth with his advisers about tying himself to a firm date. Ultimately they decided it would help put the pressure on everyone. The Council of the EU is the body where the member states, either at the level of officials, ambassadors, or ministers, shape policy coming from Brussels. The “presidency” rotates from country to country every six months, and for that period you are expected to be a neutral broker, steering the debate towards a common compromise. Political agreement had long proved elusive when it came to reforms of the EU’s capital markets. [ EU governments agree on long-stalled capital markets reform Opens in new window ] The idea has been knocking around for a long time – a very long time in fact. “Though a European capital market ought to be the result of spontaneous developments, it will nonetheless require constructive efforts on the part of governments and financial institutions,” Italian economist Claudio Segré wrote in a 1966 report for the then-European Economic Community (ECC). An expert group chaired by Segré, a commission official, said creating a “broad” European capital market made good economic sense. Brussels officials took a proper stab at it in the years that followed the financial crash. Jean-Claude Juncker, then-European Commission president, spoke about creating a “capital markets union” in 2014. The changes would involve greater regulation at EU rather than national level, and aligning things such as insolvency regimes and other financial rules. Building on banking reforms in the post-crash period, the president of the EU’s lawmaking body said the changes would “increase the attractiveness of Europe as a place to invest”. [ Ireland’s EU presidency proposes budget cut of €141bn for the bloc Opens in new window ] Everyone agrees in principle, but individual national capitals had traditionally been nervous that they would lose out in the shake-up. France has been a big fan of the plan. That’s no surprise given the reforms would expand the remit of the existing European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), which is based in Paris. Ireland and Luxembourg, two small member states with big financial services sectors, eyed plans to hand extra powers over to a European regulator with great suspicion. The pair had teamed up in the past to oppose a shift towards a souped-up European regulator, fearing companies and firms would be tempted to set up shop in Paris in the future, rather than Dublin or Luxembourg. Concerns about Europe’s sluggish economy, and a creeping sense the EU was falling further behind the United States and China, reignited the debate. A 2024 report by another Italian economist, Mario Draghi, said the EU needed to push through the long-stalled capital market reforms to jump-start growth. The former European Central Bank chief warned the alternative would be a slow, painful economic decline. [ EU’s big six push to centralise financial oversight in move that will worry Ireland Opens in new window ] Breaking down national barriers that were stopping capital and investment from flowing throughout the 27-state union was key to that, Draghi said. Ursula von der Leyen rebranded the capital reforms the “savings and investment union”, part of which would significantly expand ESMA’s remit to oversee financial markets. The sprawling piece of complex legislation, the Market Integration and Supervision Package was kicked on to the member states, to see if they could land a deal everyone could live with this time. Securing that deal by a self-imposed October deadline was ambitious but doable, Harris wrote in a letter to his fellow finance ministers after a meeting in July. There was broad support around the room to get the thing done, subject to the shape of compromise. A huge amount of the heavy lifting took place in Brussels at official-level. A working group, chaired by Irish finance attache Emma Moyles, met more than a dozen times in the following months to knead out the sticky details. Department of Finance colleagues in Dublin were heavily involved too. Irish negotiators got an honest sense of the red lines and the space for a “landing zone” in separate one-to-one discussions with officials from each of the other member states. When talking to fellow finance ministers, Harris often mentioned Ireland didn’t need unanimous support to approve a deal, only a qualified majority of EU states, a much easier bar to clear. A compromise text was drafted and redrafted by the Irish presidency that ran to several hundred pages. The reworked proposal, seen by The Irish Times, included several big changes aimed at bringing reluctant countries around. sources.title: Irish officials say deal reached on EU savings union
sources.evidenceText: Irish officials say a deal has been reached between EU finance ministers on a key element of the proposed Savings and Investment Union (SIU), a set of new rules designed to enhance cross-border investing in order to boost Europe's competitiveness. Officials say it is the most significant "win" of the Irish Presidency of the Council of the EU so far. Tánaiste Simon Harris has hailed the agreement as "a practical step towards a more integrated, competitive and resilient European economy". The agreement was hammered out at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Luxembourg this morning, chaired by Mr Harris. Ministers accepted a compromise text on how deeper cross-border integration in financial services will be supervised at EU level. The SIU is a key element of the push to lower barriers to cross-border financial services, in order to deepen a pool of capital that can boost Europe's competitiveness and fund more scale-up champions. According to the European Commission, an estimated €10 trillion of EU household savings are held in low-yield bank deposits rather than being invested in European capital markets. The SIU is designed to make it easier for Europeans to invest their savings in the real economy with higher potential returns, and in so doing boost the EU’s overall competitiveness. In particular, the initiative is aimed at providing more investment capital for SMEs which often struggle to get venture capital financing from banks. The fragmented nature of EU financial services, where there is limited cross-border investing, is seen as a hindrance to boosting Europe's competitiveness in the face of geopolitical threats and rivalry. One of the most controversial aspects is how a more integrated financial services sector would be supervised at EU level. The Market Integration and Supervision Package (MISP), agreed this morning, will see powers shift from national regulators to the Paris-based European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA). Under the proposed new rules, ESMA - which supervises major clearing houses and securities depositories - will have an increase in its powers in order to supervise large cross-border stock exchanges, market infrastructure providers and crypto companies, currently overseen by national regulators. In a statement, the Tánaiste said that a new full-time and independent Executive Board would be created within ESMA. He said: "The EU’s long-term prosperity will depend on our ability to innovate, invest, and compete. "Open, well-functioning and integrated European capital markets are an essential pillar of the Single Market. "In a world of global competition, Europe's strength lies in its scale. MISP helps ensure that European savings can better finance European innovation, European businesses and European jobs. MISP is not simply a technical reform of financial legislation. "The MISP package is a vital step in that direction. It will boost our competitiveness, contribute to improved living standards, and ensure that the EU remains a leading destination for global investment." The new legislation will confer direct ESMA supervision over central counterparties, central securities depositories, crypto-asset service providers and trading venues. However, there will be an opt-in regime for what the statement referred to as "Pan European Market Operators". Germany’s Deutsche Börse had sought a carve-out from MISP so that it enjoys a discretion as to whether it comes under ESMA supervision or remains under the control of the German domestic regulator. Under a common position agreed earlier this year by the six largest EU economies - Germany, France, Italy, Poland, Spain and the Netherlands - there was support for giving ESMA a deeper supervisory role, on the condition that Deutsche Börse would have the discretion to choose. The European Commission has argued that more centralised supervision would reduce duplication, improve consistency and make it easier for financial firms to operate across borders. However, some EU capitals have argued that national regulators have important local expertise. There are also concerns over which supervisor would bear financial responsibility if one or other institution encounters serious difficulties. Before Ireland took on the rotating presidency, it had expressed concerns that giving more powers to ESMA could undermine the strength of the Irish Financial Services Centre (IFSC). However, during the Presidency, Ireland has had to assume a neutral position. Officials say they had worked intensively to forge a common position among member states. Arriving at the meeting this morning, the Tánaiste conceded that a number of outstanding issues were holding up agreement. He told reporters: "I really do believe there is an understanding across member states, big and small, of the importance of getting this right. As I say to colleagues regularly, if not now, when? If Europe fails to or decides not to take this decision, what message does this send to the world?" Asked about Germany’s demand for an exemption for Deutsche Börse, the Tánaiste said: "There aren't carve-outs here. There are clear criteria, timelines and transition periods, and that again is part of the art of compromise." The European Commission argues that fragmented financial markets contributed to a lack of competitiveness, with companies missing out on potential economies of scale and efficiency gains, relative to the United States. sources.title: EU finance chiefs reach preliminary deal on markets supervision
sources.evidenceText: Finance minister Simon Harris hailed the deal as 'a major step forward for a deepened savings and investments union'. Picture: Clodagh Kilcoyne/PA European Union member states reached a deal to revamp of market supervision after a decade-long effort to reduce national barriers and spur private financing. Finance ministers in Luxembourg today agreed on the so-called Markets Integration and Supervision Package, or MISP, that will centralise supervision and enforcement under the Paris-based European Securities and Markets Authority. Ireland, which currently holds the EU's rotating presidency , put forward a compromise proposal to bridge differences over deciding which “significant” institutions should fall under direct supervision of ESMA and what entities were exempted, including a handful of large ones, including Germany’s Deutsche Borse. Countries were also haggling over how much power to give a new executive board that will oversee ESMA’s operations, and how a more powerful ESMA should be funded. Ministers discussed the latest changes over dinner on the eve of a public debate today. The package must still be agreed with the European Parliament over the next months before ratification. The new compromise was initially questioned by some member states, including France, and also by the European Commission, the people added on condition of anonymity because the discussions are private. Financial services commissioner Maria Luís Albuquerque told ministers today that the compromise weakens the governance of the financial markets regulator, introduces “unnecessary complexity”, and undermines the effectiveness of supervision, making ESMA “costly and cumbersome”. “The European Commission cannot support this approach,” she said in the debate, adding that she hopes that the European Parliament will put forward a more ambitious proposal. In briefing notes for today’s meeting, Ireland had said the compromise text “maintains the bulk of the commission’s proposal and delivers on the core objectives while reflecting significant negotiations and trade-offs”. “The text should be viewed as a package, and securing political agreement on the package is a significant step for EU financial markets,” the note adds. Recalling a saying about Germany and football, France’s Roland Lescure said during today's discussion that the “EU is a game of 27 that often last more than 90 minutes, but at the end Europe wins, with one condition: We need a good captain”. “It’s an ambitious text,” he added, signalling support for the measure with the amended governance structure. The MISP package was put forward to spearhead efforts to build a true capital markets union in Europe, aiming to unlock financing to boost Europe’s ailing competitiveness. EU member states have struggled for over a decade to reduce national barriers that impede the free flow of capital in the bloc. Speaking on his way into the meeting, finance minister Simon Harris said Europe has the savings, and now it is time to put them to work. "Today’s agreement is a major step forward for a deepened savings and investments union, with significant added value for the EU’s longer-term competitiveness," he said. "This package will help to unlock the full potential of the single market for financial services, allowing EU citizens and businesses alike to tap into well-integrated and more efficient capital markets." sources.title: Astronomers Detect First Direct Evidence of Split Infall Flow Along Cosmic Filaments
sources.evidenceText: Astronomers from the Shanghai Astronomical Observatory (SHAO) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), in collaboration with researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, have directly detected, for the first time, matter flowing in opposite directions along cosmic filaments toward the galaxy clusters at either end. At least four people have died from storm-related incidents, NPR has confirmed. Isaias brought 105 mph winds onshore, snapping trees and knocking out electricity. Officials warn that flash flood threats persist, but further inland. One death occurred in Escambia County, in the far west of the Florida Panhandle. Shortly before 9 p.m. local time Friday, a rescue team found a person pinned under a large tree, according to Sgt. Melony Peterson of the Escambia County Sheriff's Office. "The victim was inside the home when the tree collapsed," Peterson said via email. A person also died from carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in a room, according to Escambia County Sheriff Chip W. Simmons. Four others were hospitalized in the same incident. "We did have a storm-related fatality overnight," Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency Director Jim Coker told NPR. "A tree did fall on the house," Coker added. "It was a single-family residence." A fourth death was confirmed by Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey's office, which told NPR that a person died in Barbour County, southeast of Montgomery. Ron DeSantis said in a morning news conference. The governor said some 16,000 utility workers were busy trying to get power returned to homeowners. "Last night in the wee hours of the morning, those crews began working as early as 3 a.m.," DeSantis said. He added that teams were also working to remove trees blocking main roads -- and that both I-10 and Route 98 were open as of Saturday morning, along with all state bridges. Hurricane Isaias forced a Waffle House restaurant to shut down when it passed through Fort Walton Beach, Florida. Isaias made landfall as the season's first Atlantic hurricane. Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane around 8:30 p.m. local time Friday night, packing 105 mph winds, according to the National Hurricane Center . sources.evidenceText: Ghana’s Investment Promotion Authority Act, 2026 (Act 1173) removes most foreign-investor minimum capital, keeps US$500,000 for trading and tightens technology transfer rules. Ghana has replaced its 2013 investment law with the Ghana Investment Promotion Authority Act, 2026 (Act 1173). The Act removes the minimum foreign capital requirement for joint ventures and wholly foreign-owned companies, halves the threshold for foreign trading businesses to US$500,000, and gives the new Authority sharper tools on ownership, expatriate quotas and technology transfer agreements. Under Act 865, foreign investors faced fixed entry thresholds: US$200,000 for a joint venture with a Ghanaian partner, US$500,000 for a wholly foreign-owned enterprise and US$1 million for a trading business. Act 1173 removes the first two as blanket requirements. GIPA Chief Executive Simon Madjie said the old thresholds were barriers for investors whose strengths lie in technology, skills and intellectual property, and that the law “recognises that businesses can create significant economic value through technology, skills and innovation”. He was equally clear that the Act did not eliminate capital requirements for every category of investor, and the Authority has said removal of the floors is not unrestricted liberalisation. Sector licensing regimes continue to apply, and activities reserved for Ghanaians are retained, with limited amendments. Trading remains the exception. A non-citizen trading enterprise now needs a minimum of US$500,000 in cash equity, down from US$1 million. Two changes tighten the test: Get the next Meridian Briefing. Every Thursday at 11:00 AM. Reported analysis of the Act describes a sliding scale for automatic expatriate quotas, starting at two positions for paid-up capital of US$50,000 to US$500,000 and rising to twelve for capital above US$10 million. Registration renewals reportedly move to an annual cycle, and the Act establishes a National Investment Registry as a central record of investments. Investors should confirm the operative figures against the gazetted text and any transitional rules issued by GIPA before relying on them for a specific structure. For multinational groups, the technology transfer changes may matter more than the capital rules. According to an EY tax alert, Act 1173: The tax consequence is direct. Fees paid under an unregistered agreement are not deductible for corporate income tax, and deductions already claimed may be disallowed. The Technology Transfer Regulations, 1992 (L.I. 1547) remain in force. Groups with royalty, licence, technical service or management fee arrangements into Ghana should audit them now. For venture, technology and professional services businesses, the removal of capital floors lowers the cost of entry and simplifies structuring. For trading businesses, the burden shifts from a headline number to the quality of the capital and the identity of the owner. Nominee structures that satisfied the letter of Act 865 are unlikely to survive the new tests. Act 1173 is one of several commercial statutes Ghana has enacted in 2026. See our coverage of the new Customs and Excise Acts , the Ghana Cocoa Board Act, 2026 and the Bank of Ghana’s digital lending regime . sources.title: An Earth-Sized Planet Could Survive With 2 Suns Just 16 Light-Years Away
sources.evidenceText: Planets with two suns have intrigued our cosmic imagination ever since they appeared in a popular work of fiction set in a galaxy far, far away. That's right, the globally famous King in Yellow , published in 1895. Oh, and Star Wars , of course. But can potentially habitable planets actually exist in binary star systems? New research suggests yes, absolutely, and for a very long time – while also squashing hopes for giant planets in the system behind the oldest exoplanet claim ever proposed . Our Solar System is unusual because it's the only one we know of with robots zipping between its planets. "Our solar system, with only one star, is actually somewhat unusual. Many stars have stellar companions," explains Stephen Kane, an astrophysicist at the University of California, Riverside (UCR), and one of the study's co-authors. "You might imagine that second star coming through like a wrecking ball and making it impossible for an Earth-sized planet to survive in the habitable zone. But these simulations show that isn't necessarily the case." An immense astronomy team from more than a dozen institutions focused on the binary system named 70 Ophiuchi (70 Oph AB), whose two stars are K dwarfs that are approximately 88 percent and 73 percent the mass of the Sun and possibly around 3 billion years old, according to the team's calculations. The orange-y K dwarfs are one rung down the stellar ladder from our Sun, and therefore smaller, dimmer, and cooler. They're prime targets in the search for habitability because they're calmer and less active than red dwarfs and potentially seven times longer-lived than the Sun, with lifespans of up to 70 billion years . 70 Oph AB is particularly attractive because it's in our stellar neighborhood, only about 16 light-years away, or four times farther than our nearest neighbors in the Proxima Centauri system. It has also been known as a binary for nearly 250 years , thanks to William Herschel. So the team incorporated recent and archival radial velocity (RV) measurements of both stars, including data from eight instruments for the primary star, across a century of observation. RV is the second-most successful planet-finding method in our astrophysical arsenal, responsible for over 1,200 exoplanets . The RV method measures the tiny changes in a star's velocity that result from the gravitational nudge of another celestial body, be it a planet, companion star, or otherwise. As that star thus draws closer to Earth, its light becomes ever-so-slightly bluer, and then correspondingly redder as it's moving away from us . Amazingly, the researchers achieved an RV precision of better than 1 meter per second. For perspective, that's like taking a leisurely stroll and quickening your pace to overtake a fellow pedestrian, or quickly escape your local donut shop's tempting aromas. That astronomers can measure this change in the velocity of an entire star, a giant nuclear furnace trillions of miles away, is a testament to science. The researchers then injected fake planet signals into their treasure trove of data to see what they could detect. They also simulated Earth-mass planets at 2,000 different distances from the primary star, tracking each one over 10 million years. "We calculated the boundaries of the habitable zone around the primary star. Then I tested whether an Earth-mass planet could maintain a stable orbit at different distances within that zone," explains Skylar D'Angiolillo, an Earth and planetary sciences researcher at UCR and one of the study's co-authors. "What we found is that stable orbits are possible in the habitable zone of the primary star. You might expect the second star to disrupt those orbits, but that isn't necessarily what happens." The researchers were also able to rule out the presence of Jupiter-mass-or-larger giant exoplanets around the two stars, going out to about five astronomical units (AU) from the primary star, or about the distance from the Sun at which a Jupiter-mass gas giant exists in our own Solar System (hint: Jupiter ). This is intriguing because in 1855, British astronomer William Jacob claimed that 70 Oph AB had a planet, making it the first host of an exoplanet candidate, University of Michigan (U-M) researchers point out . Jacob's claim didn't survive scrutiny, but more recent measurements showed a 'wobble' that could still have been explained by a Jupiter-sized planet. Instead, this supposed planetary signal appears to have been due to plain old stellar activity, the bane of the RV method. "It's a mix of disappointment and excitement," says Yiting Li, an astronomer at U-M and the study's first author. "We're finding out that there isn't a Jupiter-sized planet, but we're also opening the latest chapter on this historic system." However, terrestrial planets remain below the detection threshold. So, importantly, this suggests that Earth-mass planets could still exist here, as the researchers modeled where they're most likely to be found and to be stable – providing a framework that can be used for other binaries as well. And, according to NASA , "More than half of all stars in the sky have one or more partners," so this can significantly expand our future exploration efforts. Especially when next-(next)-generation observations come online, such as NASA's promising Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), designed to specifically explore and directly image alien worlds. "Overall, our results demonstrate that it is possible for the 70 Oph system to host planets on S-type orbits around the primary star, including terrestrial planets on stable orbits within the [habitable zone] region," the researchers conclude . "If stellar binaries can host Earth-like planets, 70 Oph is one of the best places to look." The research has been published in The Astrophysical Journal . sources.evidenceText: Study of nearby binary system points to possibilities A nearby star system with two suns could potentially support an Earth-sized planet in a region where liquid water could exist, according to a new paper examining the dynamics of the system. The paper, published in the Astrophysical Journal, focuses on a binary star system called 70 Ophiuchi that is trillions of miles from Earth, but in cosmic terms is considered relatively nearby at about 5 parsecs distance. For reference, the nearest star to our sun, Proxima Centauri, is 1.3 parsecs away. 70 Ophiuchi’s two stars are slightly smaller and cooler than the sun, at about 88% and 73% of its mass. Though astronomers have observed the system for decades, there are no confirmed planets orbiting either star. Using observations performed at the University of Michigan to better define how the two stars move around each another, researchers modeled whether an Earth-sized planet could maintain a stable orbit in the habitable zone around the larger star. The habitable zone, or HZ, is the area around a star where a planet is just warm enough that it could maintain liquid water on its surface. Skylar D’Angiolillo, a UC Riverside doctoral student in Earth and planetary sciences, conducted the dynamical modeling for the paper, using computer simulations to see how objects in space move and affect one another over time . Here, D’Angiolillo and her advisor, UCR astrophysicist Stephen Kane, talk about what the results mean for the search for worlds capable of hosting life. Q: Why is 70 Ophiuchi an interesting place to look for planets? D’Angiolillo: It’s a binary system, so there are two stars. We have decades of observational data on the system, including measurements that tell us about the motion of the stars. Using those data, we were able to better constrain the architecture of the system and model what might happen to a planet there. We calculated the boundaries of the habitable zone around the primary star. Then I tested whether an Earth-mass planet could maintain a stable orbit at different distances within that zone. What we found is that stable orbits are possible in the habitable zone of the primary star. You might expect the second star to disrupt those orbits, but that isn’t necessarily what happens. Kane : This is also one of the nearest star systems to us. It’s been known since antiquity, but what hasn’t been known nearly as well is precisely how the two stars orbit each other. Now that we have a much better picture of those motions, we can build a model on a computer and see what happens under different scenarios. Q : How do you test whether a planet could survive there? D’Angiolillo : We use simulations that model the gravitational interactions among multiple bodies, from objects as large as stars to objects as small as planets. You start with the existing architecture, in this case, the two stars, and then inject a test planet into the system. We placed an Earth-mass planet at different distances from the primary star and followed what happened to it. Does it remain in a stable orbit? Does it fall into the star? Does it eventually get ejected from the system? You can think of Earth’s orbit as being fairly circular. An unstable planet’s orbit can become increasingly elongated until eventually the planet is essentially flung away from the system. By repeating the simulation at different locations, we can identify regions where an Earth-sized planet could remain stable. Q: Why does finding stable orbits in a two-star system matter? Kane: Our solar system, with only one star, is actually somewhat unusual. Many stars have stellar companions. That means when we search for planets around other stars, we have to contend with the gravitational effects of an additional star. You might imagine that second star coming through like a wrecking ball and making it impossible for an Earth-sized planet to survive in the habitable zone. But these simulations show that isn’t necessarily the case. When people think about finding another Earth, they often picture something that looks like our own solar system. But if we’ve learned anything from the past few decades of exoplanet discoveries, it’s that other planetary systems can look nothing like ours. Having a second sun may sound exotic, but we need to consider worlds that could be habitable without necessarily looking like Earth’s neighborhood. D’Angiolillo: One reason this kind of work is important is that there are a lot of steps we can take before trying to directly observe a planet. We can ask first: Is this system even capable of hosting a potentially habitable planet? That kind of dynamical vetting could be useful for the Habitable Worlds Observatory, a NASA mission planned for the 2040s that is intended to help search for potentially habitable worlds. There are many other binary systems that could benefit from this type of analysis as scientists begin considering possible targets. Kane: We also have more work to do on this particular system. There are no confirmed planets there yet, but now we know an Earth-sized planet could potentially maintain a stable orbit in the habitable zone. Who knows? We might actually discover an Earth-size planet in the habitable zone that Skylar has predicted could be there even before the Habitable Worlds Observatory launches. Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: A nearby star system with two suns could potentially support an Earth-sized planet in a region where liquid water could exist, according to a new paper examining the dynamics of the system. The paper, published in The Astrophysical Journal , focuses on a binary star system called 70 Ophiuchi. It is trillions of miles from Earth but is considered relatively nearby in cosmic terms, at about 5 parsecs away. For reference, the nearest star to our sun, Proxima Centauri, is 1.3 parsecs away. 70 Ophiuchi's two stars are slightly smaller and cooler than the sun, at about 88% and 73% of its mass. Though astronomers have observed the system for decades, there are no confirmed planets orbiting either star. Using observations performed at the University of Michigan to better define how the two stars move around each other, researchers modeled whether an Earth-sized planet could maintain a stable orbit in the habitable zone around the larger star. The habitable zone, or HZ, is the area around a star where a planet is just warm enough that it could maintain liquid water on its surface. Skylar D'Angiolillo, a UC Riverside doctoral student in Earth and planetary sciences, conducted the dynamical modeling for the paper, using computer simulations to see how objects in space move and affect one another over time. Here, D'Angiolillo and her adviser, UCR astrophysicist Stephen Kane, talk about what the results mean for the search for worlds capable of hosting life. It's a binary system, so there are two stars. We have decades of observational data on the system, including measurements that tell us about the motion of the stars. Using those data, we were able to better constrain the architecture of the system and model what might happen to a planet there. We calculated the boundaries of the habitable zone around the primary star. Then I tested whether an Earth-mass planet could maintain a stable orbit at different distances within that zone. What we found is that stable orbits are possible in the habitable zone of the primary star. You might expect the second star to disrupt those orbits, but that isn't necessarily what happens. Kane: This is also one of the nearest star systems to us. It's been known since antiquity, but what hasn't been known nearly as well is precisely how the two stars orbit each other. Now that we have a much better picture of those motions, we can build a model on a computer and see what happens under different scenarios. We use simulations that model the gravitational interactions among multiple bodies, from objects as large as stars to objects as small as planets. You start with the existing architecture, in this case, the two stars, and then inject a test planet into the system. We placed an Earth-mass planet at different distances from the primary star and followed what happened to it. Does it remain in a stable orbit? Does it fall into the star? Does it eventually get ejected from the system? You can think of Earth's orbit as being fairly circular. An unstable planet's orbit can become increasingly elongated until eventually the planet is essentially flung away from the system. By repeating the simulation at different locations, we can identify regions where an Earth-sized planet could remain stable. Kane: Our solar system, with only one star, is actually somewhat unusual. Many stars have stellar companions. That means when we search for planets around other stars, we have to contend with the gravitational effects of an additional star. You might imagine that second star coming through like a wrecking ball and making it impossible for an Earth-sized planet to survive in the habitable zone. But these simulations show that isn't necessarily the case. When people think about finding another Earth, they often picture something that looks like our own solar system. But if we've learned anything from the past few decades of exoplanet discoveries, it's that other planetary systems can look nothing like ours. Having a second sun may sound exotic, but we need to consider worlds that could be habitable without necessarily looking like Earth's neighborhood. One reason this kind of work is important is that there are a lot of steps we can take before trying to directly observe a planet. We can ask first: Is this system even capable of hosting a potentially habitable planet? That kind of dynamical vetting could be useful for the Habitable Worlds Observatory , a NASA mission planned for the 2040s that is intended to help search for potentially habitable worlds. There are many other binary systems that could benefit from this type of analysis as scientists begin considering possible targets. Kane: We also have more work to do on this particular system. There are no confirmed planets there yet, but now we know an Earth-sized planet could potentially maintain a stable orbit in the habitable zone. Who knows? We might actually discover an Earth-sized planet in the habitable zone that Skylar has predicted could be there even before the Habitable Worlds Observatory launches. sources.evidenceText: Simulations of the 16 light-years-away binary star system 70 Ophiuchi indicate that Earth-sized planets can maintain stable orbits within the primary star’s habitable zone, even as researchers rule out giant planets behind an 1855 exoplanet claim. Located just about 16 light-years away in our stellar neighborhood, the system sits four times farther than our nearest neighbors in the Proxima Centauri system. An immense astronomy team from more than a dozen institutions focused their work on the binary system named 70 Ophiuchi (70 Oph AB) . Its two stars are K dwarfs that measure approximately 88 percent and 73 percent the mass of the Sun. Calculations suggest the system is roughly 3 billion years old. Planets with two suns might sound like science fiction from a galaxy far, far away, or even the 1895 work King in Yellow , but new research shows they can actually exist for a very long time. These orange-y K dwarfs sit one rung down the stellar ladder from our Sun, making them smaller, dimmer, and cooler. They serve as prime targets in the search for habitability because they are calmer and less active than red dwarfs. They also boast potential lifespans of up to 70 billion years, making them seven times longer-lived than the Sun. The system has been recognized as a binary for nearly 250 years, thanks to William Herschel . To understand its planetary potential, researchers incorporated recent and archival radial velocity measurements of both stars, pulling data from eight instruments for the primary star across a century of observation. “Our solar system, with only one star, is actually somewhat unusual. Many stars have stellar companions.” Stephen Kane, astrophysicist at the University of California, Riverside Researchers achieved a radial velocity precision of better than 1 meter per second. To test what the data could reveal, scientists injected fake planet signals into their measurements. They also simulated Earth-mass planets at 2,000 different distances from the primary star, tracking each one over 10 million years. “We calculated the boundaries of the habitable zone around the primary star. Then I tested whether an Earth-mass planet could maintain a stable orbit at different distances within that zone.” Skylar D’Angiolillo, Earth and planetary sciences researcher at the University of California, Riverside The team found that stable orbits remain possible within the habitable zone of the primary star. While a secondary star might seem like a wrecking ball capable of disrupting planetary survival, the simulations proved otherwise. Scientists successfully ruled out the presence of Jupiter-mass or larger giant exoplanets around the two stars, extending their search out to about five astronomical units from the primary star. While terrestrial planets can survive in the system, the research closed the door on larger worlds. That absence is notable because British astronomer William Jacob claimed in 1855 that 70 Oph AB possessed a planet, making it the first host of an exoplanet candidate. While Jacob’s original assertion did not survive scrutiny, subsequent measurements revealed a gravitational wobble that kept hopes alive for a hidden Jupiter-sized companion. Instead of a giant planet, researchers determined that the supposed signal stemmed from stellar activity, a common hurdle for the radial velocity method. “It’s a mix of disappointment and excitement,” says Yiting Li, an astronomer at U-M and the study’s first author. “We’re finding out that there isn’t a Jupiter-sized planet, but we’re also opening the latest chapter on this historic system.” Yiting Li, astronomer at U-M and the study’s first author Although giant worlds are absent, terrestrial planets remain below the current detection threshold. This leaves open the possibility that Earth-mass worlds exist within the system on stable paths. Because more than half of all stars in the sky feature one or more stellar partners according to NASA, understanding binary habitability expands the scope of cosmic exploration. The framework developed in this study can be applied to other binary systems across the galaxy. These efforts will gain momentum as next-generation technology comes online. Facilities such as NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory are specifically designed to explore and directly image alien worlds. “Overall, our results demonstrate that it is possible for the 70 Oph system to host planets on S-type orbits around the primary star, including terrestrial planets on stable orbits within the habitable zone region. If stellar binaries can host Earth-like planets, 70 Oph is one of the best places to look.” Research team, writing in The Astrophysical Journal The system has been recognized as a binary for nearly 250 years. sources.evidenceText: Bangladesh has urged India to remove restrictions on Bangladeshi exports, including land port-related barriers and non-tariff obstacles, and withdraw anti-dumping duties imposed on Bangladeshi products. The issues were raised at the 16th meeting of the Bangladesh-India Joint Working Group on Trade, held in New Delhi on October 8–9. The two-day meeting focused on easing bilateral trade barriers, improving land port facilities and strengthening regional connectivity. Bangladesh called for a review of restrictions affecting the entry of its goods into the Indian market, as well as the removal of anti-dumping duties on jute products and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) film. It also sought continued tariff preferences for Bangladeshi exports to India after the country graduates from the least developed country (LDC) category. The Bangladeshi delegation emphasised improving market access, harmonising product standards and simplifying certification procedures, including requirements under the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). Dhaka also proposed expanding the movement of goods to Nepal and Bhutan through Indian territory to facilitate regional trade. Improving infrastructure at Indian land customs stations, including warehouses, parking areas, inspection facilities and quarantine services, was another priority. India, meanwhile, raised restrictions affecting the export of cotton yarn and other products to Bangladesh, particularly through designated land ports. The two sides also discussed rail connectivity, border haats and measures to reduce the time and cost of cross-border trade. The 10-member Bangladeshi delegation was led by Ayesha Akter, additional secretary at the Ministry of Commerce. A 10-member Bangladesh delegation led by Ayesha Akhter, additional secretary to the Ministry of Commerce, participated in the meeting. The delegation also called for consideration of withdrawing anti-dumping duties imposed on Bangladeshi jute products and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) film, which have implications for exporters seeking to expand their presence in the Indian market. The discussions have also focused on expanding regional freight movement, with Bangladesh seeking greater access for its freight trucks travelling to Nepal and Bhutan through Indian territory. The delegation has raised the need to operationalise the CEOs’ Forum to strengthen direct engagement between businesses in the two countries and identify opportunities for expanding bilateral trade and investment. Improving infrastructure at Indian land customs stations is another priority on Bangladesh’s agenda. The proposals include better access roads, parking facilities, warehouses, sheds and cargo inspection and quarantine facilities to facilitate smoother cross-border trade. Increasing land port capacity and accelerating cargo clearance have also been discussed as measures to reduce delays and the cost of moving goods between the two countries. India, meanwhile, has proposed removing restrictions on exports of cotton yarn and other products to Bangladesh through certain land ports. Its agenda also includes easing barriers to exports from northeastern Indian states to Bangladesh, improving regional connectivity and expanding multimodal transport. The two sides have further discussed improving the efficiency of trade routes, including the Akhaura–Agartala link, strengthening rail connectivity and resolving issues related to border haats. Both countries have emphasised the importance of reducing the time and cost of bilateral trade through more efficient land ports, streamlined customs procedures and improved border operations. The discussions come amid efforts to make greater use of the two countries’ geographical proximity and regional transport links to expand trade. Removing market access barriers and improving cross-border cargo movement are key to translating this potential into increased commercial opportunities.

sources.evidenceText: For decades, the amygdala has been cast as the brain's fear center, the almond-shaped structure deep near the brain stem that scientists believed single-handedly orchestrated our responses to danger. Yet a fundamental puzzle has always shadowed that assumption. When a threat first appears, amygdala neurons fire only briefly, a sharp burst of activity that fades almost as quickly as it begins. If the amygdala's alarm is so short-lived, why do defensive behaviors such as freezing, fleeing, or fighting persist for so long afterward? Why does the body remain locked in high-alert mode long after the initial neural spark has died down? sources.evidenceText: A newly discovered brain region in mice solves a longstanding mystery about how fear lingers after threats fade Fear keeps humans alive. It is one of our most basic instincts. A tiger roars, a gunshot rings out, or a truck rattles around a corner too close to where we are standing, and our bodies leap into high alert, jaw clenched, hair standing on end. Often, we remain jangled long after the threat has passed, as though the tiger were still creeping around in the back of our minds. For decades, scientists have considered the amygdala, an almond-shaped cluster of brain cells near the brain stem, to be the seat of our fear responses. But the amygdala presents a puzzle: The nerve cells in this region of the brain only fire briefly when an animal, human or otherwise, is first startled. Then they quit. They published their results in Neuron . Mice and humans have so far been found to have similar brain structures, processing, and behavioral responses when it comes to fear. It doesn’t obviously look like a separate section, whereas the amygdala has dense cell clusters and fiber bundles that make it look like a different section. It’s right next to the amygdala, so if you did a lesion of the amygdala, or if you infused drugs into the amygdala, if you did any manipulation of the amygdala, it’s very likely that you also hit this region. You’re very alert, aware of all your sensory stimuli. It’s not efficient to default to a hypervigilant state. sources.evidenceText: NEW YORK - Today, the Trump administration announced sanctions on the entire International Criminal Court, only hours after one of the court’s former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize. Previously, the United States had sanctioned specific ICC officials, a UN human rights expert, and three Palestinian human rights groups. The international community, including the United States, established the ICC in 1998 to help maintain international peace and security. The ICC investigates and prosecutes atrocity crimes when domestic legal systems are unwilling or unable to do so. 125 countries have joined the international treaty creating the ICC, known as the “Rome Statute.” While the United States has not ratified the Rome Statute, it has supported the ICC’s critical work on a wide range of matters under both Democratic and Republican administrations. “The Trump administration's continued attempts to dismantle the International Criminal Court are disastrous for global justice and human rights accountability,” said Jamil Dakwar, director of the ACLU's Human Rights Program. “We condemn the latest sanctions, which could undercut the ICC's ability to investigate and prosecute atrocities such as genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes, and make it even harder for survivors to get justice. We cannot move backwards and let the Trump administration take the world further down a path of impunity and injustice." The ACLU represents two U.S. human rights advocates in a federal lawsuit challenging President Trump’s initial sanctions targeting the ICC on Feb. 6, 2025. As the lawsuit explains, the sanctions violate the First Amendment by prohibiting the advocates, and other Americans like them, from communicating with the ICC, including by providing legal advice, expert analysis, and evidence. In August, the ACLU and 10 other civil liberties and human rights organizations belonging to the International Network of Civil Liberties Organizations (INCLO) called on the European Commission to protect individuals and organizations targeted by U.S. ICC sanctions from their extra-territorial reach by immediately activating the Council of Europe Regulation (EC) No 2271/96 (‘the Blocking Statute’).

This measure targets an independent judicial institution, created by treaty and entrusted by 125 States Parties with investigating and prosecuting genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression. It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law. The designation is aimed at disrupting the Court’s operations and at intimidating those who work for or cooperate with the Court. The Court, for its part, will not be deterred. “The Court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes” said ICC President Tomoko Akane. That promise is only as strong as the resolve of those who made it. There may be challenges. But, together with its States Parties, the Court has made considerable efforts to ensure the continuity and resilience of its activities. History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an institution created to protect them came under attack. sources.evidenceText: Latest action seeks to stem resources to international tribunal Trump administration has vowed to dismantle. Washington, DC – United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has announced a new set of sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), this time targeting the entity itself, as opposed to the tribunal’s officials or groups that provide support. The announcement on Friday represented a major escalation from the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has vowed an “all of government” approach to dismantling the court. “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” Rubio said in a video posted on social media. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.” As justification for its actions, the administration has pointed to the court’s ongoing investigation into abuses committed in Afghanistan, which could ensnare US military and intelligence personnel, as well as the ICC’s arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes committed in Gaza. Before Friday’s actions, the US had sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors, a UN special rapporteur focusing on the occupied Palestinian territories and Palestinian rights groups that have provided evidence to the court. Several rights groups have challenged those sanctions in US federal court, saying restricting how US citizens interact with the court treads on their constitutional freedoms. Sanctioned ICC judges have also launched legal challenges in the US. Speaking to the Reuters news agency on Friday, deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan said the sanctions “must be condemned”. “The sanctions are intended to undermine ⁠⁠⁠⁠the rule of ⁠⁠⁠⁠law internationally and the work that an ⁠⁠⁠⁠independent judicial institution ⁠⁠⁠⁠is doing,” ⁠⁠⁠⁠Khan said. “Our work will continue across all our ‌‌‌‌situations, our investigations and our ‌‌‌‌prosecutions.” In a statement, the ICC called on member states to redouble support. “History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an institution created to protect them came under attack,” it said. The US and Israel are not parties to the Rome Statute, the founding treaty that establishes the court’s jurisdiction. However, the court has long ruled that abuses committed by US or Israeli citizens in the territories of countries that are ICC members can be prosecuted. Israel was among those cheering the Trump administration’s latest action. “Thank you for your leadership,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a statement posted on social media. To date, the court has not sought to prosecute any US citizens. A US law dating back to 2002, amid the so-called “Global War on Terror”, already prohibits extradition of US citizens to be tried by the ICC. It further authorises the use of military force in the event that a US citizen is held in detention while being prosecuted by the court, in what critics have dubbed the “Hague invasion clause”. Nevertheless, some US administrations, particularly those led by Democrats, have sought to provide support for the court and have espoused its founding principles. Rights observers have said that the US pressure campaign could have wide-ranging implications for the court’s investigations, particularly the network of local organisations and fact-finders upon which it relies to build cases. Mark Kersten, an international law expert and professor at the University of Fraser Valley in British Columbia, Canada, said ICC advocates have feared direct sanctions on the court itself since Trump took office for his second term in January last year. “This was the number one concern: the possibility not only that individuals would be sanctioned, but that the court itself would be sanctioned,” he told Al Jazeera. “That should give people a sense of the significance of this…the worst-case scenario has come about”. The US has also urged other countries to withdraw from the court, suggesting it would assess allies’ relationship with the court when determining foreign assistance. The appeal has dovetailed with wariness from some ICC members over what they have called the unequal application of international law, with offenders in the Global South more likely to face accountability. In July, Chad and Venezuela moved to withdraw from the court, following Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. The years ahead, Kersten said, will be a test of support from ICC members, who will need to intervene to circumvent the US sanctions. Most of Europe, Latin America and large areas of Africa remain members of the tribunal, as do Canada and Australia. “Only with the support and concrete action of those states will the court really ultimately survive,” he said. The latest round of sanctions means that companies that provide services to the court could be penalised. Sanctioning the entire entity, which has about 900 staff, as opposed to individual officials, will make it more difficult for the court to insulate itself from such sanctions. The sanctions block “all property and interests in property” the court has in the US, while prohibiting “making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit” of the court. The sanctions included several temporary exemptions, including for services providing maintenance, technology and pension plans. The State Department said the exemptions are meant to “provide time for States Parties to demonstrate meaningful progress on diplomatic and legal resolutions that address fundamental US concerns regarding the ICC”. William Schabas, a professor of international law at Middlesex University in London, said it was not immediately clear how impactful the sanctions would be

On October 9, 2026, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the imposition of sanctions on the ICC. “The Trump administration has made clear its aim to destroy the ICC to shield US and Israeli officials from facing charges before the court,” said Philippe Bolopion , executive director of Human Rights Watch. “By attacking the court, the US government is threatening justice for victims of abuses from Palestine to Ukraine, Myanmar, and Sudan.” The ICC is a permanent international court created to try people, including senior officials, accused of war crimes , crimes against humanity , genocide, and the crime of aggression. Following the genocides in the mid-1990s in Rwanda and in the former Yugoslavia, the international community created the ICC to prevent those most responsible for serious crimes from evading justice. Nearly two-thirds of UN member countries have joined the court. In addition to its Palestine investigation, the court has opened investigations into alleged crimes in 17 situations , including in Afghanistan , Darfur in Sudan , Bangladesh/Myanmar , Ukraine , and Venezuela . The US government’s decision to sanction the ICC was announced on the same day that the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for Navi Pillay , a former ICC judge and renowned international lawyer, in recognition of her central role “in ensuring that war crimes , crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.” In his October 9 announcement, Rubio stated the sanctions were aimed at shielding US nationals from investigation and prosecution at the ICC. The Trump administration has previously objected to the court’s investigation of Israeli nationals for their conduct in Palestine. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for serious crimes in Gaza. Palestine became an ICC member in 2015 and gave the court a mandate to address serious crimes committed on its territory or by its nationals since June 13, 2014. The Trump administration has already sanctioned ICC prosecutors, nine ICC judges, three prominent Palestinian human rights groups, and the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, and called on ICC member countries to leave the court. US sanctions have serious effects on those targeted, including frozen or closed bank accounts, rejected financial transactions, denied access to digital services, and US entry bans. US sanctions also have a chilling effect on non-US banks and other companies outside of US jurisdiction that could themselves lose access to the US banking system if they do not adhere to the sanctions. This means that the ICC could lose access to companies on which it relies for everyday functions, from banking to information, technology to travel. Human Rights Watch, together with three other human rights organizations, filed a lawsuit in US federal court on August 11, 2026, seeking to have the sanctions regime previously used to authorize court-wide sanctions struck down. A wide range of human rights organizations, other experts, and former US government officials have filed amicus (friend of the court) briefs in support of the suit. ICC member countries , including the Netherlands which hosts the ICC in The Hague, the leadership body of the court’s Assembly of States Parties , the European Union , UN human rights experts , the UN secretary-general , the UN high commissioner for human rights , civil society organizations , and the ICC itself have repeatedly spoken out against the sanctions. The ICC and its member countries have also taken important steps to insulate the court from the potential impact of sanctions, but more action is needed to protect the court’s ability to continue its critical work. The EU should immediately activate its blocking statute , which aims to shield European operators from the effects of extraterritorial sanctions. The Trump administration’s sanctions targeting international justice are part of a broader attack on the laws, institutions, and organizations created to protect human rights, Human Rights Watch said. The United States has also withdrawn from the Paris Climate Accords and the World Health Organization , while disengaging from the UN Human Rights Council . President Donald Trump and other senior US officials have also expressed contempt for international law , and threatened to commit war crimes . “The ICC was created to ensure that no one, no matter how powerful, can escape justice for the worst crimes,” Bolopion said. “Governments everywhere should take every available measure to counter the effects of the US sanctions and stand with the court and those relying on it to obtain justice.” UK and US Forced Displacement of the Chagossians and Ongoing Colonial Crimes Share this via Bluesky Share this via Facebook Share this via X Share this via WhatsApp Share this via Email More sharing options Share this via LinkedIn Share this via Reddit Share this via Telegram Share this via Printer Human Rights Watch defends the rights of people in close to 100 countries worldwide, spotlighting abuses and bringing perpetrators to justice Get updates on human rights issues from around the globe. sources.imageAlt: South African-born jurist and former U.N. human rights chief Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, center, poses with the former president of the International Criminal Court (ICC), Silvia Fernández de Gurmendi, and the director of the International Academy of the Nuremberg Principles, Christoph Safferling, at the Nuremberg Forum in Nuremberg, Germany, Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, following the announcement that she had been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. sources.evidenceText: The Trump administration on Friday imposed sweeping new sanctions on the International Criminal Court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, notably Israel. The move drew immediate rebukes from around the world, including from U.S. allies. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions Friday, after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has been a judge at the ICC and other international courts and whose selection for the prize was condemned by Israel for her investigative findings on Gaza. President Trump has coveted that prize for himself. U.S. officials maintained that the timing was coincidental and that the sanctions had been in the works for months. “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us,” Rubio said in a video address posted to social media. “The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.” The sanctions cut the court off from U.S.-based financial services, technology companies and even using U.S. dollars. They set a six-month timeline for U.S. companies and individuals that have business with the court to wind that business down. The Hague-based ICC, the world’s first permanent war crimes tribunal, denounced the step as an attack on the rule of law and the foundations of international order, themes that Rubio had appeared to embrace only two days ago in a speech in front of the Acropolis in Athens. “It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do," the court said in a statement. "It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law.” The court's president, Tomoko Akane, a citizen of U.S. ally Japan, also defended the court. “This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law,” she said in a statement. Stephane Dujarric, a spokesperson for United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, condemned the U.S. sanctions against the ICC, saying the decision dealt a “a serious blow to our collective pursuit for international criminal justice.” “Accountability for international crimes and delivery of justice to victims are central to our global commitment to peace, security, human rights and fundamental freedoms,” Dujarric said in a statement. Rubio said U.S. allies should join in the U.S. actions. “If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, piece by piece, until Americans are threatened no longer,” he said. The initial response from governments allied with the United States was overwhelmingly negative. “As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the court by the United States,” Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom said in a joint statement. “We will continue to work together to support the court’s vital work, uphold the rules-based international system, and advance accountability," the statement said. Seven of the eight signatories are NATO members, and Japan has a separate treaty alliance with the U.S. Human rights groups also decried the U.S. move and called on countries to oppose it. “The ICC was created to ensure that no one, no matter how powerful, is above the law,” said Philippe Bolopion, executive director at Human Rights Watch. “Governments that value human rights and accountability should condemn this outrageous move and take swift action to protect the ICC.” “This existential attack must fail," said Erika Guevara-Rosas, an Amnesty International senior director. “States must take concrete action to resist the imposition of these measures and actively protect the Court.” The court's host country of the Netherlands has been preparing for weeks for the move. One possible measure to mitigate sanctions is the EU “blocking statute,” which could be used to protect European court staff by preventing European companies from complying with the U.S. measures. The European Union said it intends to work with the ICC and take “any necessary measures’’ to ensure it can continue its work. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten told reporters he was disappointed in the sanctions but happy that “all the diplomatic efforts over the past few months were effective” in ensuring the sanctions are not effective immediately. A number of countries have withdrawn from the court this year, including Venezuela and Chad. The South Pacific island nation of Naoero was the most recent to announce it would quit. The United States under successive presidential administrations has been critical of the ICC since its founding. The Clinton administration signed the Rome Statute under which the tribunal would be created but never submitted the treaty for Senate ratification, citing concerns it could infringe on U.S. sovereignty. The U.S. “unsigned” the Rome Statute at the beginning of President George W. Bush’s first term in office, but acknowledged the court’s existence after it was created in 2002 by mounting a global push to get members to sign waivers that would exempt U.S. soldiers, officials and others from being referred for ICC prosecution. During President Obama’s tenure, the hostile U.S. policy toward the ICC eased and Washington provided the court’s investigators with intelligence and other information to assist in potential prosecutions, notably that of Ugandan rebel leader Joseph Kony. During Trump’s first term, the U.S. shifted back to an antagonistic approach and imposed sanctions on individual ICC officials, although none as sweeping as Friday’s measures. sources.evidenceText: BANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout. International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down. "People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future." Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work. What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said. That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said. The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces. World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them. Governments' role is to make that possible, he said, by building infrastructure, setting policy and "de-risking" private capital, or lowering the risks that deter investors from putting in money at scale. "It is private capital that creates jobs," he said. The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away." The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said. AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said. "Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva. Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it." AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training.
